name: Ḍomaaki
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Yoshioka, Noboru. 2022. Eat a Spoonful, Speak a Night Tale: A Ḍomaaki (Hi)story Telling. Bulletin of the National Museum of Ethnology 46(4): 565-592. DOI 10.15021/00009894 (Minpaku repository PDF).
catalog_quote: Ḍomaaki has the two-way pitch accent: high or middle. It is unclear whether the accent system is distinctive. Every word has a high pitch on one of the syllables. Herein, I put an acute accent mark on the high-pitched vowel (V́) in multisyllabic words, whereas I omit it from monosyllabic words as surface forms, where the only vowel must take an accent.
world_status: statement found in an open source

Herein, I put an acute accent mark on the high-pitched vowel (V́) in multisyllabic words, whereas I omit it from monosyllabic words as surface forms, where the only vowel must take an accent.
new_statements.translation: (Supporting statement, same author, Japanese) Yoshioka 2025, p. 2: 「語彙的に位置の決まっている高いか高くないかの二段階ピッチアクセントがあるが弁別性は確認できていない．唯一母音にアクセントが置かれる単短音節語以外では高アクセントの置かれた母音に鋭アクセント記号を付して V́ とした．」 = 'There is a two-level pitch accent, high vs. non-high, whose position is lexically fixed, but its distinctiveness has not been confirmed. Except in monosyllabic short-vowel words, where the only vowel carries the accent, the vowel bearing the high accent is marked with an acute, V́.'

Herein, I put an acute accent mark on the high-pitched vowel (V́) in multisyllabic words, whereas I omit it from monosyllabic words as surface forms, where the only vowel must take an accent.' Verbatim match with the reported quote and locator. Surrounding section: it is Yoshioka's phonemic tr…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Every word carries one high-pitched (accented) syllable; the position is lexically determined (not derivable from a positional rule), realised as a high vs. mid pitch contrast; whether the accent is contrastive is not yet established. Tikkanen 2011: 207 adds that in several noun paradigms the stress accent shifts to the final stem vowel or the first vowel of the ending, may move to the last mora of a final long vowel (giving a rising tone), and that the endings -a, -ŋa, -°aaŋa (nom.pl) and -ye, -i (gen.sg) are never accented. Lorimer 1939 gives no rule (he marks 'high tone' on certain final vowels, p. 24, and finds the participial -i 'does not appear to carry a fixed stress accent', p. 107).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Yoshioka: monosyllabic words necessarily bear the accent (not marked). Tikkanen 2011 fn. 7 (p. 207): accent shifts occur especially in monosyllabic consonant-final nouns with a short stem vowel, nouns in unaccented -a, and nouns with a short accented final syllable; some nouns are treated differently by different speakers or by the same speaker at different times.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (phonemic transcription of citation and text forms); Yoshioka's data are from the Hunza (Mominabad) dialect; Tikkanen's from Hunza 1995 fieldwork. Distinctiveness of the accent is explicitly left open by Yoshioka (2022, 2025) and in his Burushaski grammar (2012, already held by the project: 'it remains unclear whether or not the pitch accent of Domaaki is distinctive').
new_statements.identity_note: All open first-hand sources describe the Hunza (Mominabad) dialect: Yoshioka 2022/2025 (consultant AAJ, Mominabad, b. 1986), Tikkanen 2011 (Mominabad fieldwork 1995), Lorimer 1939 (Hunza/Berisho). Weinreich 2008/2011 describe the Nager dialect (Domyal/Sikanderabad); Weinreich 2008 treats Hunza and Nager as two dialects but gives no separate accent statement. Recent literature (Hussain 2020; Donlay and Kiani 2025) uses the community-preferred name Dawoodi. Glottolog has only the language-level code doma1260 (no dialect codes).

sources.note: Phonology pp. 22-24 has no stress rule; 'Tones' §4 p. 24: 'I marked a high tone in the final vowel of certain verbal forms, notably in the final -a of the Infinitive, and sometimes in that of the Imperative plural, and the -i of the Past Participle Active. Scattered remarks: locative -ana stress 'sometimes on the first vowel of -ana, sometimes on the syllable preceding it' (p. 64); personal endings 'seem usually to be stressed' unless the preceding syllable is long (p. 92); participial -i 'does not appear to carry a fixed stress accent…

sources.note: §3.1 'Paradigmatic accent shift and declensions', p. 207: 'In several paradigms the stress accent shifts to the final vowel of the stem, or first vowel of the ending. In monosyllabic and diphthongal stems before consonantal endings, the accent may shift to the last mora of a final long (double) vowel, causing a rising tone.' Fn. 7: endings -a, -ŋa, -°aaŋa (nom.pl) and -ye, -i (gen.sg) are never accented; speaker variation. Hunza dialect (Mominabad 1995). No general placement rule.
